title: Meta Agrees to Pay $18 Billion and Overhaul Teen Safety in Landmark Settlement With 47 States
excerpt: The largest tech settlement in history ends a trial over youth social media addiction, requiring daily time limits, night mode, and hidden like counts for minors on Facebook and Instagram.
body:
• Meta has agreed to pay approximately $18 billion — $17 billion to 29 states that filed a joint lawsuit in 2023, plus roughly $1 billion to additional states and territories — to settle claims it designed addictive social media platforms that harmed children.
  • The settlement requires Meta to implement two-hour daily time limits for teen users, a default night mode blocking app access from midnight to 6 a.m., and the removal of features like visible "like" counts for minors.
  • District Court Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers approved the deal on Wednesday, ending a landmark trial in Oakland, California, where states had sought up to $1.4 trillion in damages.
  • Meta did not admit wrongdoing and has urged rivals TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar safety measures, making 30% of the payout contingent on competitors matching its commitments.

Largest Tech Settlement in History

Meta Platforms has agreed to pay approximately $18 billion and overhaul how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram, ending a landmark trial over youth social media addiction that attorneys general called the largest settlement with a big tech company in history.

The deal, announced Wednesday by 47 state attorneys general, resolves a pivotal legal battle that accused the company of deliberately designing features — infinite scrolling, algorithmic recommendations, and frequent notifications — to hook young users while misleading the public about the risks.

"For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health."

— Jay Jones, Virginia Attorney General

California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued Meta in 2023. The trial began just over a week ago in Oakland, California, with U.S. District Court Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers presiding. Instagram head Adam Mosseri had begun testifying Tuesday, and CEO Mark Zuckerberg was expected to take the stand before the settlement cut the proceedings short.

How the Money Breaks Down

Just over $17 billion will go to settling the joint lawsuit, with the remainder resolving claims from additional states and territories. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the money would be paid out over 10 years, with the state receiving at least $1.5 billion. New Jersey expects at least $525 million, Massachusetts at least $366 million, Virginia $353 million, and Michigan $171 million.

The funds will support state youth online safety initiatives, including after-school programs, summer activities, and digital literacy counselors, according to attorneys general.

While $18 billion amounts to a fraction of Meta's 2025 revenue of $201 billion, the settlement's structural changes could have a more lasting impact on the company's ad-driven business model.

What Changes for Teens

The agreement goes beyond financial penalties to mandate product changes across Facebook and Instagram. Meta will implement a two-hour cumulative daily time limit for users aged 13 to 17 that only parents can adjust. The company will prompt teens after every 15 minutes of continuous use to encourage breaks.

A default "night mode" will block access to the apps from midnight to 6 a.m. for minors, and a "school mode" will reduce notifications during school hours. Meta will also hide "like" counts on teens' posts by default, block "extreme makeup filters," and give teens the option to disable autoplay and switch to a non-algorithmic feed.

California Attorney General Bonta said the changes are expected to go into effect within months, with an independent auditor monitoring Meta's compliance.

A Conditional Payout

Meta built a significant condition into the deal: 70% of the settlement fund will be paid in annual installments over the next decade, but the remaining 30% — roughly $5.4 billion — will only be paid if YouTube and TikTok agree to make similar payments to states and adopt comparable safety changes.

"Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta. We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that's why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard."

— Meta, in a blog post

Meta did not admit wrongdoing as part of the settlement. The company called on its competitors to implement the same framework, a move North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson described as an attempt to level the playing field.

What Comes Next

The settlement does not end Meta's legal exposure. The company still faces hundreds of lawsuits from individuals, families, and school districts accusing it of addicting and harming children. Meta lost two similar cases earlier this year — one from New Mexico's attorney general that resulted in nearly $1 billion in damages, and another brought by a teen identified as K.G.M. that yielded $6 million in joint damages for Meta and YouTube.

Advocates welcomed the protections but said federal legislation is ultimately needed. "We cannot truly protect all children and teens until these protections are required on every platform and are permanent — that's something only Congress can do," said Sacha Haworth, executive director of The Tech Oversight Project.

For parents who have long raised concerns about their children's time on social media, the settlement marks a concrete, if partial, step. Whether it fundamentally changes how teenagers interact with social media will depend on enforcement, how quickly Meta implements the changes, and whether competitors follow suit.
